title: possibility of resource reservation features
body:
### What would you like to be added?

What about the possibility of resource reservation? For example, in an online cluster with rescheduling capabilities, or when certain nodes (due to node maintenance or eviction from the cluster) need to be taken offline for some operational tasks. Suppose we have an online cluster with hundreds of nodes, and we use node labels to differentiate resource pools for different business units. If today I need to decommission a specific node or several nodes within a particular resource pool, I would need to "migrate" the pods on those nodes (i.e., evict the pods so they can be rescheduled to other nodes in different pools). We want to safely migrate the online services, so we are looking for a mechanism similar to "resource reservation." We want to preemptively reserve certain resources on the nodes before the pods are created, ensuring that our high-priority pods can definitely be scheduled successfully.

### Why is this needed?

For some high-priority pods, we want them to remain intact during node maintenance, which is very important to us. If we cannot preempt them, we will not evict them. 
I know this seems to be a very complicated problem in a large cluster, and I may not have considered it comprehensively. Or if there is already a similar feature, that would be great.

body:
### What happened?

When configuring api server authentication using oidc  as per https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#json-web-token-authentication, I'm observing the unhelpful error message

`2026-02-09 15:21:41     ERROR   filters/authentication.go:75    Unable to authenticate the request      {"component": "vcluster", "error": "invalid bearer token", "errorCauses": [{"error": "invalid bearer token"}]}`

Turning verbose logs with -v9 did not help
Adding audit logs for tokenreviews did not help either.

By dichotomy and trial and error, finally identified the root cause being the `"email_verified": false` claim. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Expecting the following friendly trace to be printed (which was observed with < 1.34)

`ERROR   filters/authentication.go:73    Unable to authenticate the request      {"component": "vcluster", "error": "[invalid bearer token, oidc: email not verified]"}`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

starting api server with:
```
--oidc-issuer-url=https://...
--oidc-client-id=kubeapi-client
--oidc-username-claim=email
```

and the OIDC ID token in the JWT bearer token containing
```json
{                                                                                                                     
  "exp": 1770650801,                                                                                                                                                                   
  "iat": 1770650501,                                                                                                                                                                   
  "auth_time": 1770650218,                                                                                                                                                             
  "jti": "d9661afa-...",                                                                                                                                       
  "iss": "....",                                                           
  "aud": "kubeapi-client",
  "sub": "ac133c7f-...",
  "typ": "ID",                                                                                                                                                                         
  "azp": "kubeapi-client",
  "sid": "d554a5ed-...",
  "at_hash": "HRn...",
  "acr": "0",             
  "email_verified": false,                                                                 
  "name": "redacted",         
  "preferred_username": "redacted@my-corp.org",                                        
  "given_name": "redacted",
  "family_name": "redacted",   
  "email": "redacted@my-corp.org"                                                   
}                           
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The requirement that email_verified=true is hard to discover from documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#json-web-token-authentication which does not hint it, see https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/27c169c468ba07bcd4ee6594a4ab9fec75096d10/content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication.md?plain=1#L309-L327

> (JWT) compliant tokens. JWT authentication mechanism is used for the ServiceAccount tokens that Kubernetes itself issues,
> and you can also use it to integrate with other identity sources.
> 
> The authenticator attempts to parse a raw ID token, verify it's been signed by the configured issuer.
> For externally issued tokens, the public key to verify the signature is discovered from the issuer's public endpoint using OIDC discovery.
> 
> The minimum valid JWT payload **must** contain the following claims:

>   "aud": ["my-app"],              // at least one of the entries in issuer.audiences must match the "aud" claim in presented JWTs.

However, claims other than `email` will be prefixed with the issuer URL to prevent naming clashes with other plugins. | sub | No |

title: Job readiness gates
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An alternative to `Job.spec.suspend` that allows multiple controllers to cooperate towards starting a Job.

This is analogous to scheduling gates https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-scheduling-readiness/

### Why is this needed?

This would enable queueing of steps of a workflow.

For example, the job could have:
```
readinessGates:
  - kueue.k8s.io/suspend
  - snakemake.io/step
```

The job is only allowed to run (create pods) if all gates are removed.
In the case above, `snakemake.io/step` would be removed by snakemake when all the dependencies for this job are completed.

At this point, kueue would allow this job to compete for resources in the queue. When there is enough quota to run this job, Kueue would remove the `kueue.k8s.io/suspend`.

title: apimachinery scheme initialization matches only on kind
body:
### What happened?

### Summary

We have a CRD `experimental.io/v1alpha1/APIGroup`. We're using `kube-state-metrics` to emit metrics for the custom resources, but are receiving the following type mismatch error:
```
expected type *unstructured.Unstructured, but watch event object had type *v1.APIGroup
```

The root cause is that dynamic informer uses global scheme to decode objects. If custom resource's `Kind` matches a native kubernetes `Kind`, the scheme returns the native type regardless of the group or the version. The flow is as following:
1. `kube-state-metrics` discovers CRD `experimental.io/v1alpha1/APIGroup` and sets up a dynamic informer that expects type `*unstructured.Unstructured`.
2. The dynamic informer uses the global scheme to decode objects. During scheme initialization, my custom resource matches a native kubernetes kind `v1.APIGroup` (https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery@v0.34.0/pkg/apis/meta/v1#APIGroup).
3. However, the dynamic informer expects `*unstructured.Unstructured`, causing a type mismatch error.

### Detailed Flow

**1. Discovery Phase**

In `kube-state-metrics/internal/discovery/discovery.go`, it uses a dynamic informer to watch for new CRDs. When a new CRD is added, it parses the CRD spec and stores the discovered GVKs (group, version, kind, plural) in its internal map.

```
factory := dynamicinformer.NewFilteredDynamicInformer(client, schema.GroupVersionResource{
    Group:    "apiextensions.k8s.io",
    Version:  "v1",
    Resource: "customresourcedefinitions",
}, "", 0, nil, nil)
informer := factory.Informer()
```

**2. Dynamic Client Creation**

When `kube-state-metrics` wants to interact with custom resource, it creates a dynamic client. This `resourceClient` is a `dynamic.ResourceInterface`, which is used to list, watch, get, and manipulate resources.

```
client := dynamic.NewForConfig(config)
resourceClient := client.Resource(schema.GroupVersionResource{
    Group:    "experimental.io",
    Version:  "v1alpha1",
    Resource: "apigroups", // plural
})
```

**3. Listing/Watching Resources**

When `kube-state-metrics` wants to list or watch custom resource objects, it calls methods like the following. These methods are implemented in `client-go/dynamic/simple.go` and ultimately make HTTP requests to the Kubernetes API server.

```
resourceClient.List(ctx, listOptions)
resourceClient.Watch(ctx, watchOptions)
```

**4. Deserialization via Global Scheme**

When the API server sends an object (e.g., custom resource), `client-go`’s dynamic client receives the raw JSON. It then calls the global scheme to decode the object.

The scheme tries to find a Go type for the given GVK. If the Kind matches a type registered in the scheme (i.e., `v1.APIGroup`), even if the group/version are different, it will instantiate that native type.

```
func (s *Scheme) New(kind schema.GroupVersionKind) (Object, error) {
	if t, exists := s.gvkToType[kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}

	if t, exists := s.unversionedKinds[kind.Kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}
	return nil, NewNotRegisteredErrForKind(s.schemeName, kind)
}

func (s *Scheme) Decode(data []byte, gvk *schema.GroupVersionKind, into Object) (Object, *schema.GroupVersionKind, error) {
    // ...
}
```

**5. Type Mismatch Error**

The dynamic informer expects all objects to be of type `*unstructured.Unstructured`. But because the scheme found a native type for kind `APIGroup`, it deserializes the object as `*v1.APIGroup`.

When the informer’s event handler runs, it tries to cast the object to `*unstructured.Unstructured`, and hence causing the error:

```
expected type *unstructured.Unstructured, but watch event object had type *v1.APIGroup
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Scheme initialization should only return a match if the `group` also matches:

```
func (s *Scheme) New(kind schema.GroupVersionKind) (Object, error) {
	if t, exists := s.gvkToType[kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}

	// NEW CHANGES
	if t, exists := s.unversionedKinds[kind.Kind]; exists {
		// find a gvk in gvkToType with the same Kind and Group
		for gvk := range s.gvkToType {
			if gvk.Kind == kind.Kind && gvk.Group == kind.Group {
				return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
			}
		}
		// if no matching group, do not fallback to Kind-only
	}

	return nil, NewNotRegisteredErrForKind(s.schemeName, kind)
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
import (
	"testing"

	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestIssue(t *testing.T) {
	nativeGVK := schema.GroupVersionKind{Group: "meta", Version: "v1", Kind: "APIGroup"}
	nativeGV := schema.GroupVersion{Group: "meta", Version: "v1"}
	customGVK := schema.GroupVersionKind{Group: "experimental.io", Version: "v1alpha1", Kind: "APIGroup"}

	// register the native Kubernetes APIGroup type
	scheme := runtime.NewScheme()
	scheme.AddKnownTypeWithName(nativeGVK, &metav1.APIGroup{})
	scheme.AddUnversionedTypes(nativeGV, &metav1.APIGroup{})

	// create a scheme for the custom gvk
	obj, err := scheme.New(customGVK)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	// UNEXPECTED: assert that custom gvk matched native gvk, regardless of group or version
	_, ok := obj.(*metav1.APIGroup)
	require.True(t, ok)
}
```

### What would you like to be added?

We have seen a common use case that user uses HPA controller that talks to a metrics server (an extension apiserver).

This issue is very non-trivial for users to understand and troubleshoot. In order to make users have a better experience and also hide some unnecessary complexity from users. I want to propose to adding additional default APF config as mentioned above.

title: API Server Keeps Using Open TCP Connections to Terminating Admission Controller Pods
body:
### What happened?

I am encountering an issue where the Kubernetes API server continues to use open TCP connections to an admission controller pod after it has been marked as unready and removed from the service endpoints.

### My Setup

- I have a `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` pointing to my service `admission-controller`, which uses an `ignore` failure policy.
- The `admission-controller` deployment consists of multiple pods, each running an HTTP server. The service selector targets all pods in the deployment, leading to multiple endpoints.
- Upon pod termination, the goal is to perform a graceful shutdown by:
  - Marking the pod as unready.
  - Waiting until the pod is removed from the service endpoints.
  - Handling inflight messages before shutting down the pod.
 
### The Issue
Once a pod is marked as unready, it is correctly removed from the service endpoints and does not receive new connections—this is expected behavior.
However, the pod continues to receive HTTP requests over old open TCP connections. 

This leads to two major problems:

1. I cannot close the TCP connections on the server side because it may result in a potential loss of requests from the API server.
2. There is no defined deadline for when the connection gets closed on the client side, leaving it open indefinitely unless manually terminated.

Additionally, I discovered that the API server does not retry requests (and opens a new TCP connection) if it encounters a closed connection.

### Stress Test Results
I performed a test to further diagnose the issue:

1. Deployed one `admission-controller` pod in the deployment (intended to block all requests).
2. Ran the following command: 
   ```kubectl rollout restart deployment admission-controller```
   - A new pod was created, and the old pod began terminating.
   - The old pod closed the server as soon as it became unready.
4. Sent 1000 requests to create a pod to simulate stress.

#### Expected Result
No pods should be created, as the `admission-controller` should block all the requests.

#### Actual Result
Some pods were created during each run. There appears to be a small window of time where the cluster is unprotected, and the API server does not receive a response because of the failurePolicy (ignore). As a result, it proceeds with pod creation.

### Impact
This is particularly concerning because during that window where old TCP connections are still in use, the API server can bypass the admission controller, leading to potential security risks.

### What I’ve Tried
I attempted to gracefully handle the shutdown by waiting for connections to close naturally, but I am unable to define a clear deadline or force the API server to retry on connection closure.


Any assistance or guidance on how to address this issue would be greatly appreciated.

### What did you expect to happen?

1. The TCP connections used by the API server should have a reasonable time-to-live, allowing the pod to wait long enough to ensure all existing TCP connections are properly closed upon termination.
2. I expect the API server to have a built-in retry mechanism to handle such failures.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As mentioned above using the described setup and stressed tests.

title: owned Custom Resources not garbage collected after CRD API version removal
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:

We are trying to deprecate and remove some CRD API versions and as part of that to ensure that users who have originally deployed Custom Resources at the legacy versions can upgrade.
For a Custom Resource X that is a dependent on another Custom Resource Y and they both have been originally created using a legacy API version `v1alpha2`, we observe that after an upgrade to a controller version where `v1alpha2` is no longer served, X is not garbage collected after Y has been deleted.

X after the upgrade:
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: CertificateRequest
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/certificate-name: test1
...
name: test1-4d8sc
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1alpha2
    blockOwnerDeletion: true
    controller: true
    kind: Certificate
    name: test1
    uid: a20001e7-4793-42bf-955a-a6216cbdc933
...
```

Y after the upgrade:
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
...
  name: test1
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "12276"
  uid: a20001e7-4793-42bf-955a-a6216cbdc933
```

In the above config `CertificateRequest.metadata.ownerReferences[0].apiVersion` is incorrect. I thought that perhaps this is the issue, so I tried editing it `v1alpha2` -> `v1` just before running the delete command. The edited `CertificateRequest` was still not deleted.
Does the `metadata.ownerReferences[0].apiVersion` matter- I seem to remember seeing somewhere on #sig-api-machinery Slack that it is not actually used?

#### What you expected to happen:

I expected that X would be deleted after Y is deleted as it happens normally with these resources.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):
1. Deploy `cert-manager` version `v0.16` where the storage version for all CRDs is `v1alpha2`
2. Create an `Certificate` (Y) Custom Resource using the `v1alpha2` API. A `CertificateRequest` X will be created for Y with Y set as X's owner reference.

title: DaemonSet controller fails to recreate Pods
body:
### What happened?

When a DaemonSet is created, the DaemonSet controller attempts to create the required Pods on each node. However, if the initial Pod creation is interrupted (e.g., a Mutating Admission Webhook adds a deletionTimestamp immediately after creation), the Pod enters the terminating state before it can be fully scheduled or observed as running.

In this case, the DaemonSet controller observes the deletion event and calls:

`dsc.expectations.DeletionObserved(logger, dsKey)`
(see code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b236451928797b544423a73bfb67b6846178e3b1/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L530)

This satisfies the expectation for that particular Pod, but no new Pod creation is triggered because the controller only attempts to create missing Pods during full reconciliation (e.g., when the DaemonSet spec changes or the controller resyncs). If the DaemonSet object itself remains unchanged, the controller will not attempt to create a replacement Pod, even though the previous Pod was never successfully running.

As a result, the DaemonSet can remain in a broken state with fewer Pods than desired, and the missing Pods are never recreated.



### What did you expect to happen?

The DaemonSet controller should continue attempting to create new Pods to satisfy the desired number of replicas on each node, even if the initial Pod creation was interrupted and the Pod was immediately terminated (e.g., by a webhook setting deletionTimestamp).

Ideally, the controller should treat such a case similarly to a failed Pod creation or a Pod that was deleted before becoming ready — and trigger a new creation attempt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Mutating Admission Webhook that adds a deletionTimestamp to every newly created Pod (for demonstration purposes only).

-  Example: a simple webhook that patches /metadata/deletionTimestamp with metav1.Now() on CREATE operations.

2. Create a DaemonSet (any simple DaemonSet, e.g., using busybox image with a sleep command).
3. Observe that:

- The webhook immediately adds deletionTimestamp to the Pod.

- The Pod enters Terminating state and is deleted.

- The DaemonSet controller observes the deletion and calls DeletionObserved(), satisfying the expectation.

- No new Pod is ever created on that node, even though the DaemonSet still has missing replicas.

### Anything else we need to know?

1. This behavior occurs because the DaemonSet controller relies heavily on the expectations mechanism to avoid over- or under-creation. When a deletion is observed, it clears the expectation without triggering a new creation attempt unless the DaemonSet object is updated or the periodic resync occurs.

2. We believe there should be a safety mechanism to handle abnormal cases like this (e.g., webhook-induced immediate termination). One possible solution is:

- After expectations expire (TTL) or when a deletion is observed without the Pod ever being ready, force a reconciliation to attempt creating a new Pod.

- Alternatively, track whether the Pod was ever in a "running" or "scheduled" state before deletion, and if not, treat it as a failed creation and retry.

title: HPA development is not active
body:
/sig autoscaling
/cc @kubernetes/sig-autoscaling-misc 

## What

HPA's development has not been active recently.
It causes many PRs to struggle to get reviews, including some KEPs.
Essentially, this is the problem of lacking approvers in HPA.

## Context (AFAIK)

Currently, @mwielgus is the only approver, but already left the sig-autoscaling chair, and I'm not sure if they're still willing to help in reviewing.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/OWNERS#L7
I know the step down doesn't always mean a stop working on things, but, in this case, actually the last review from them was more than 1 year ago.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+reviewed-by%3Amwielgus+is%3Aclosed

There are some minor changes made in HPA though, all of them are approved by someone else (root approvers), not stamps from sig-autoscaling.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commits/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler

Also, @gjtempleton is trying to take over the position, and he's (only) a reviewer (not yet approver) apart from @mwielgus now.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124607
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124661

## Proposal

We're trapped in a vicious cycle; HPA development is not active because of the lack of reviewers/approvers, and no reviewer is newly born because HPA development is not active.

There's (probably, AFAIK) no other active person who is eligible for the reviewer/approver of HPA based on [the official criteria](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/community-membership.md). 
But, we shouldn't keep the current situation, and I'd propose having some volunteers to join reviewers/approvers to break through (even if they're not officially eligible).

Regarding the approver, I cannot come up with any idea other than asking @gjtempleton to be an approver and start approving some PRs. (... I know they're also busy though)  
Also, when I was doing the container-based HPA enhancement, I remember @pbarker also helped reviewing a lot, might be a good idea to ask them to join the reviewer list. ([PRs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Apbetkier+is%3Aclosed), [reviews](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+reviewed-by%3Apbetkier+is%3Aclosed+label%3Asig%2Fautoscaling)) I can also help in being a reviewer too. ([PRs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Asanposhiho+is%3Aclosed+label%3Asig%2Fautoscaling), [reviews](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pulls?q=is%3Apr+reviewed-by%3Asanposhiho+is%3Aclosed+label%3Asig%2Fautoscaling+))

### What would you like to be added?

1. Why doesn't the k8s community have a feature to list pods by namespace index when listing pods from apiserver cache?
2. When I try to implement the pod namespace index, I see "we don't support multiple trigger functions defined". What's the reason?

### Why is this needed?

In our cluster, the number of some resources like pods are very large(100k+). When listing a namespace resources like pods from apiserver cache, the apiserver process will firstly get all the resources in all the namespaces and then filter the resources by namespace predicate even it's a very small request. title: Informer Cache RW Lock Contention Causes DeltaFIFO Backlog and Cache Staleness in KCM.
body:
### What happened? ### Summary: The Kubernetes Controller Manager (KCM) Informer caches experiences read/write mutex contention at scale. KCM controllers frequently acquire a read lock on the Informer cache to list objects from the store, which can starve the CacheController's DeltaFIFO processing from acquiring a write lock to update the Store/Cache during high throughput. This contention can lead to a backlog in DeltaFIFO, delaying delta event processing and stale cache. ### Impact A high backlog in DeltaFIFO results in stale Informer cache data, affecting KCM controllers that rely on it for resource reconciliation. This can lead to incorrect decisions, such as unnecessary resource creation or unnecessary load to APIServer and etcd from KCM Controllers. More details of impact/analysis on Statefulset controller, DaemonSet Controller is provided later in the example section. ### Code Flow : 1. Cache controller [processLoop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L205-L216) pops from DeltaFIFO queue to [processDeltas](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L552-L584). 2. As cache controller processes deltas, it [adds](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L571) or [updates](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L566) the store based on[ ADD/UPDATE etc events ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L564) from DeltFIFO queue. 3. For Add/Update operations to store, it acquires lock [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L236-L242) to update the store. 4. Meanwhile controller, in the process of [listing pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d386d6880e57556f7fe19e65e89f60501aa0aa25/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go#L314) , it acquires read lock on store [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L296-L310) while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the store at the same time. I believe [Delete in Store](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L244-L251) is also prone to this, this code path was not exercised in the test. ### Mutex pprof for KCM showing RW and Rlock on Cache/Store from CacheController Loop and StatetfulSet controller getPodsFromList ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d3dff4d4-0e1f-41bd-8c24-bd852c565917) #### Impact/Analysis examples : ##### 1. Statefulset Controller In statefulset controller case, if/when cache is stale and Pod phase status reflects[ nil](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go#L470) in cache, even though kubelet has patched the pod to `Running` phase, Statefulset controller will keep trying to [create pods and get 409's - conflict as it exists in etcd ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b6c56e5fb530c80e3510977a752be5ce6e23a27/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L397) as this [condition](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L388) will evaluate to true When I patched the KCM Statefulset controller, I can see that just `LISTING` pods from informer cache in statefulset controller when there are lots of pods in single namespace can take upto at peak `~980 ms `, which creates a huge backlog in DeltaFIFO during this time. In Statefulset controller, in the process of [listing pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d386d6880e57556f7fe19e65e89f60501aa0aa25/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go#L314) , it acquires read lock on Store [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6549f52b97d4d0837d9d0c2c1758320b19b38472/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go#L296-L310) while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the Store at the same time ( will cover on this more below) ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8904f4cf-140b-4b17-b750-b8c04ea7d8f1) **Example of DeltaFIFO backlog** ``` 12 trace.go:236] Trace[410148869]: "DeltaFIFO Pop Process" ID:kube-system/kube-proxy-fv428,Depth:229809,Reason:slow event handlers blocking the queue ... (total time: 321ms): ``` ##### 2. DeamonSet Controller : In DS conttoller it does similar thing , [listing all pods from cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6d0ac8c561a7ac66c21e4ee7bd1976c2ecedbf32/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L702) holding a read lock, which blocks all that time from updating the store in Process Deltas. Consequence of stale cache can make DS controller to create more DS pods for same node. ### What did you expect to happen? Ideally Controllers should be isolated from each other to avoid noisy neighbor problem, which isn't possible due to Controllers sharing Shared InformerCache. **Long Term**: Food for thought: - Introduce a dedicated Indexer/Cache solely for DeltaFIFO writes and syncing it in a separate routine to a separate Indexer/Store for controllers to read from can reduce lock contention from list from downstream controllers. - However, this means controllers will operate on slightly delayed data, which is much better than super stale data at scale, we need to ensure this copy is light weight unlike Huge lists that controllers do today which worsens the contention. This will help APIMachinery code has more control on these components performance instead of depending on implementations of downstream controllers. - Main thing about this theory is that - we need to ensure we are not shifting the problem to second cache to reduce overhead in first cache :) , we can something similar to what etcd does today, if difference between applies and commits b/w first cache and second cache is like say `X` , we will stop read lock to second cache from controller, to ensure second cache (i.e controller relies on) catches up to first cache, to guarantee controllers are not reading stale data - This comes with a con of increasing the memory overhead because its essentially storing a separate cache copy. This requires changing pieces of API Machinery architecture as it stands now. This approach might not only help KCM controllers but any controllers relying on caches built out of API Machinery code that runs on Dataplane Nodes. **At the minimum in short term**: - we should ensure all Controllers under KCM avoid heavy list operations on the Informer Cache/Store to reduce lock contention. - Build and utilize Indexers where applicable to minimize the number of items fetched, reducing read lock duration and improving cache update efficiency. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - Create 200 Statefulsets of 1000 pods each at once. - Ensure all those pods are Schedulable to the nodes. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version dev-dsk-hakuna-2c-2122d141 % kubectl version Client Version: v1.32.1 Kustomize Version: v5.5.0 Server Version: v1.32.2 ```

title: Add validation around Pod IP Address
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Today we make assumptions around the Pod IP address coming back from the PodSandboxStatus RPC. This RPC is responsible for returning the ip addresses to the kubelet. The assumptions we make around the current handling of pod ip addresses from containerd and crio, while they do some validation if the pod ip address exists, it possible to return an empty string as the pod ip address. It probably makes sense to do validation in the SyncPod function (link below) to ensure this scenario cannot happen. The function should fail, right now the pod is constantly scheduled without a useful error message. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4b5e40aacd021aa1485d29c4965893b3de017697/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1596

Without any validation, its possible for a pod to come up and have no ip address from the K8s perspective.

title: Ephemeral storage exhausted by users not mounting the emptyDir
body:
### What happened?

A user requested/limited ephemeral storage, but forgot to mount the emptyDir volume. The application was writing data to the snapshot of the image in containerd, which went to mounted /var/lib/containerd folder and not /var/lib/kubelet. Kubelet is watching the size of /var/lib/kubelet and was not evicting the pod, which resulted in /var/lib/containerd overfilled and node not responsive.

### What did you expect to happen?

Not sure, but current ephemeral storage mechanism is not intuitive to users. The data goes in 2 different folders and there's no control over the containerd snapshots size from kubernetes side.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Limit ephemeral storage, not create the emptyDir volume, write some data to /tmp and see /var/lib/containerd getting overfilled.

title: Feature request: Readiness Gates Controller
body:
Hi, I have a use-case for a controller that will update the pod status fields used by Pod spec readinessGates configurations.

As a platform owner, part of my responsibility is to prevent users from shooting themselves in the foot. If they fail to configure their pod spec with readiness and startup probes, their pods might be marked ready and added to the service endpoints too soon before other things beyond the user's control are fully ready to serve traffic. I'd like to have the ability to put an object in their namespace that can configure health checks against cluster objects or internal or external endpoints and update the pod status fields used by the deployment's readiness gates.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReadinessGate
metadata:
   name: platform-admin-healthcheck-ingress-pods
spec:
  healthChecks:
    - name: healthcheck-kube-object
      readinessGate: conditionType=ingressControllerHealthy
      resource:
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Deployment
        namespace: my-ingress
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            app.kubernetes.io/name: my-ingress
        status: readyReplicas>=3
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: my-app
```

For this example, my user has a deployment in some namespace which has the label `app.kubernetes.io/name: my-app`. Additionally, I as the platform admin have a deployment in the `my-ingress` namespace with the label `app.kubernetes.io/name: my-ingress` and I'm configuring a health check in the user's namespace that verifies the `readyReplicas` field on the ingress deployment is greater than or equal to 3. If it is, then the pod status conditions should have a readiness gate related `status.conditions` field with the reason `ingressControllerHealthy` added with the new condition's `status` key set to true, and otherwise it should have that field added with the `status` key set to false.

This way, I can ask the users to simply configure a pod readiness gate at their leisure to make use of the newly available fields in pod status, without needing to ask users to modify their apps nor needing build my own controller to add the pod status fields necessary to make use of the readiness gates feature.

title: Termination signals and pod/data safety impact
body:
### What happened?

Continuing discussion from slack and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115331#discussion_r1135663832

Background: Today, pod volume unmount completion is signaled by Pod deletion. We're discussing the various pod termination signals today, what controllers depend on those signals, and how they could impact pod + data safety.

> I realized that it may be better for us to make the kubelet not propagate the terminal phase until after volumes are both unmounted AND removed from the node, instead of just until they are unmounted today (deletion of the pod is blocked by removed).  i am trying to figure out a) what the real latency of removing volume mounts is on a node vs just unmounting them (even a gut check) and b) whether this is a safety issue that we glossed over before (currently terminal phase in 1.24 guarantees that the volume is not in active use, but not that the CSI plugin has had the chance to remove it) - i have no idea whether this is the case.

To answer the safety question, it is important to know that there is more cleanup after the pod volume unmount.

1. There is a global node-level mount that can be shared by multiple pods. The global mount is useful for serializing fs operations and avoiding mount limits from the node or storage backend. Cleanup only starts after all pods’ volume mounts are torn down, and this is typically where we flush data to disk (that the app has not done already). Kubelet signals completion of this by removing the volume from `Node.Status.VolumesInUse`
2. After the global mount has been cleaned up, then we can detach the volume from the node. The Attach-Detach controller waits for [pod termination signals](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18b5efceda2643b7175fbf712e8978d382077f9b/pkg/volume/util/util.go#L358) + the [global mount to complete teardown](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18b5efceda2643b7175fbf712e8978d382077f9b/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go#L214). Signaling detach completion is only possible with CSI volumes + VolumeAttachment.

How this impacts pod + data safety:
- Workload controllers can create new pods before volumes have fully completed unmount + detach. Normally this is ok because new pods will block on detach from the old node. It does result in confusing “attach failed because it’s still attached to a different node” events. 
    - If a workload uses a non-attachable volume (like NFS), this potentially could result in data inconsistency if the app is relying on the unmount to flush data to disk. But this seems unlikely for typical DBs, and in general apps using multi-writer volumes already have to take care of concurrency. 
    - There's also a misconception about RWO enforcing single-writer. It allows multiple pods scheduled to the same node to share the volume, which has caused confusion in the past especially if a workload uses something like a Deployment instead of a StatefulSet. We have [ReadWriteOncePod access mode](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2485) to address this.
- Node drain/eviction. Graceful node shutdown [doesn’t wait for volume teardon](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115148) even if there is time remaining on the shutdown timer. This can result in data loss/corruption since we don’t unmount cleanly. It could also cause pods to take longer to reschedule because instead of following the graceful volume detach flow, we trigger force detach logic after a 6 min timeout. A similar problem can happen during a node upgrade and using pod termination to signal when it’s safe to delete the VM. Actually, after https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110721, I’m not sure if the 6 min force detach will get triggered; the path for handling Node deletion could be different. This needs further experimentation/investigation.
- PVC protection controller. This feature tries to prevent the volume from being deleted while still in use by a Pod. However, it only uses Pod deletion as a signal so it could result in stale mounts left on the node if the global mount was not cleaned up yet. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94108
- Volume snapshot/cloning. We have seen disk + fs inconsistencies if you try to snapshot or clone a volume while it is in the middle of detaching. We may need to look into ways to coordinate snapshot/clone operations with detach to address this.


### What did you expect to happen?

n/a

title: Replicaset scaling down takes inter-pods scheduling constraints into consideration
body:
/sig apps
/sig scheduling
/kind feature
/assign

Want to get feedback on this proposal. I can proceed to KEP process later, if it looks worthy for it to everyone.

## Summary

Refactor Replicaset scaling down implementation for better extendability,
and take Inter-pod scheduling constraints into account during scaling down.

## Motivation

When scaling down happens, the replicaset controller determines Pod(s) to remove based on starting time etc ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826  )), but not scheduling constraints.

Inter-Pod scheduling constraints (PodAffinity/PodTopologySpread) depend on other Pods’ placement, but they’re honored only at the scheduling time.
It’d be more awesome if we can, at least, keep spreading or affinity _to some extent_ during scaling down in a vanilla kubernetes, that is, without installing [descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler) etc. 
Actually, we’ve seen _many_ issues hoping this feature; the oldest one as far as I found is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4301!

## Goal

- Refactor the replicaset controller implementation around scaling down and make it easier to implement any scaling down behavior.
  - Introduce `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin` interface and each scaling down factor is implemented as a plugin.
- Take Inter-pod scheduling constraints into account during replicaset scaling down.
  - Inter-pod scheduling constraints are only PodAffinity and PodTopologySpread for now.

## Non Goal

This proposal doesn't mean -
- Always honor those scheduling constraints during scaling down.
  - It'll just be best-effort.
- Take ALL Pods in a cluster into consideration when calculating the best Pod to remove.
  - If we did that, it'd be huge calculation cost.
- Take custom plugins into consideration.
  - Technically, it'd be possible to allow custom `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin` from users, like the scheduling framework does. But, that's out-of-scope in this proposal.

(An elaborated explanation of these Non Goal: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2054245124)

## Proposal

We’ll introduce a new interface named `ScaleDownScorePlugin`/`ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin`.

```go
type ScaleDownScorePlugin interface {
  // Score scores Pods; The higher score a Node gets, the more preferable to remove the Node, from this plugin’s pov.
  // candidatesToDelete is Pods from the replicaset, which the replicaset controller is scaling down.
  // relatedPods is all pods that are owned by any ReplicaSets that is owned by the ReplicaSet's owner.
  // ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L796 
  //
  // Each plugin’s Score() is executed concurrently.
  Score(ctx context.Context, candidatesToDelete []*v1.Pod, relatedPods []*v1.Pod) ([]*PodWithScore, error)
}

type ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin interface {
  // NormalizeScore is called after all ScaleDownScorePlugin Score() are called. 
  // A successful run of NormalizeScore will update the scores list.
  // Each plugin's NormalizeScore() is executed one by one.
  // candidatesToDelete is the aggregated result from all Score plugins.
  NormalizeScore(ctx context.Context, candidatesToDelete []*PodWithScore) error
}

type PodWithScore struct {
  Pod *v1.Pod
  TotalScore int64
}
```

1. Calculate how many Pods should be removed in the same Replicaset.
2. Call `Score` of each plugin concurrently.
3. Call `NormalizeScore` of each plugin one by one.
4. Remove Pods with higher score.

### How each plugin is implemented

We’ll implement plugins for PodAffinity / PodTopologySpread ( / [existing logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826) to determine which Pods to delete).
 
Each implementation would be like the following:

#### PodAffinity

It'll be implemented as `ScaleDownScorePlugin`.
It gives a high score to candidate Pod if a Node that the candidate Pod is running on doesn’t have a Pod matching PodAffinity of the candidate Pod.
In order to lower the cost of calculation, it’s probably better to use the scheduler’s [snapshot](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cae35dba5a3060711a2a3f958537003bc74a59c0/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/snapshot.go#L29) in the replicaset controller too.

#### PodTopologySpread

It'll be implemented as `ScaleDownNormalizeScorePlugin`.

1. Group relatedPods based on domain of topology spread
2. Calculate the total score of all Pods’ TotalScore in each domain.
3. Normalize the scores so that each domain’s total score would be similar. 

**Example:** 

Before PodTopologySpread `NormalizeScore()`:

| Domain-a (total: 600) | Domain-b (total: 300) | Domain-c (total: 3000) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| PodA: 100 | PodD: 100 | PodG: 500 |
| PodB: 200 | PodE: 100 | PodH: 1000 |
| PodC: 300 | PodF: 100 | PodI: 1500 |


After PodTopologySpread `NormalizeScore()`:

| Domain-a (total: 300) | Domain-b (total: 300) | Domain-c (total: 300) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| PodA: 50 | PodD: 100 | PodG: 50 |
| PodB: 100 | PodE: 100 | PodH: 100 |
| PodC: 150 | PodF: 100 | PodI: 150 |

Before PodTopologySpread, all Pods from Domain-c could be removed, but afterwards it’s not likely that all Pods from the same domain are removed. 

When actually implementing it, we can consider more; for example, in above case, if the controller is trying to remove 5 Pods, all Pods in domain-b could be removed at the same time. So, maybe we want to avoid "all Pods have the same score" after the normalization. (e.g., change to PodD:99 PodE:100 PodF:101)

#### Existing sorting logic

And also note that [existing logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L826) to determine which Pod(s) to remove (starting time, deletion-cost, etc) can be also implemented as ScaleDownScorePlugin.

## Risk(Downside) and Mitigation

### Negative impact to throughput of replicaset controller

Scaling down would be slower than the current implementation because of an additional calculation.

I believe it's not the hard/critical requirement to keep the current throughput of scaling **down**.
But, also, given the controller has workers that are run concurrently and are shared between scaling up/scaling down processes, we cannot say there'd be zero impact on scaling up throughput. 

We have to make sure whether the throughput (both scale up and down) is really acceptable after the implementation change.

### Backwards compatibility

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2077893254

> How will the new scores interact with pod-deletion-cost?

> What about backwards-compatibility? What if users are currently relying on the fact that the first Pod to be deleted is roughly the newest one?

If we just implement the proposal and make it the default behavior, we would break an existing scaling-down behavior.

If we concern about such breaking by this proposal, we can do, for example,

1. add a new field (or annotation) somewhere to make this behaviour non-default.
2. simplify PodTopologySpread's NormalizeScore() and make the scores returned from PodAffinity smaller than other existing algorithm's plugins.
    - simplify PodTopologySpread's NormalizeScore() > e.g., modify only scores of one Pod per domain so that at least one Pod will remain per domain.

I'd prefer (1). If we choose (2), the benefit from this proposal would be small.

## Alternative

Somehow use `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost`, but in anyways, we'd likely end up having to update Pods frequently and I didn't choose that way. 

> Users deploy controllers that update the annotation frequently causing a significant load on the api server. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/2255-pod-cost#risks-and-mitigations

(An elaborated explanation why I didn't choose deletion-cost idea: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124306#issuecomment-2071237138)

## Reference

- [Current implementation of picking Pods when scaling down](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cae35dba5a3060711a2a3f958537003bc74a59c0/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L822-L832)

title: maxSurge for node draining or how to meet availability requirements when draining nodes by adding pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A way to drain nodes by adding more pods elsewhere to meet PodDisruptionBudgets.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, when there is a Deployment, it can be configured to have a `maxSurge` to avoid going under the amount of replicas the deployment requires while allowing for a new release to be rolled out. This parameter allows adding extra pods before subtracting the old ones so that the "replicas" number required is always met as a minimum,

This feature (to my knowledge) is only available when releasing new versions of an application, however when draining nodes this would be extremely useful.

Usual cluster maintenance is done by adding new nodes before removing old ones. This means all the pods in the node need to be evicted and there is usually space for one more of each of the old node in the new node. Current solutions such as the PodDisruptionBudget or Eviction API are trying to make sure that substracting pods from the current amount don´t break anything, however the possibility of temporarily having one extra pod of each deployment is not contemplated at the moment.

This request is asking for the ability to use a surplus of pods to meet all constraints for safe eviction.

Some side notes to stress the importance. Although when operating evictions on large workloads lack of PDBs or PDBs with minAvailable/maxUnavailable settings work fine. When moving deployments with 1 replicas or HPA controlled deployments that are currently scaled down enough the problem is aggravated and can only be solved through a few inefficient means, which is acerbated if node maintenance is done automatically (such as GKE, and other cloud services)

Just in case, this is a limitation that should only be counted against Deployments with `strategy.type=RollingUpdate`.

Ways to deal with this situation currently:

1. Have a `minReplicas`/`replicas` to `>1`, and a PDB with `maxUnavailable=1` when it's known that the autoscaler if in use, it's usually scaled on the lower end. Pros: There is no downtime, Cons: Waste of resources.
2. Do nothing, and deal with eventual downtimes. Pros: No waste of resources, Cons: There is downtime in the deployment

title: Allow scaling up to meet PDB constraints
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

Currently if you have a PDB spec like `minAvailable: 1`, and a HPA defining minReplicas=1 and maxReplicas=N, you may end up in a scenario where disruptions get "stuck" if the HPA has scaled to 1. At any point an increase in load could cause the HPA to scale up to 2+, allowing the PDB to be satisfied, which leads to a weird scenario where a disruption can only occur if there is high load.

Ideally, the PDB would be able to trigger the HPA to scale up to meet constraints. For example, if I have 1 replica and a disruption is triggered, scale up a new replica first, then terminate the old one. Given an HPA is in place, I have already clearly specified I am OK with my pod being scaled up, so this shouldn't have negative impact on stateful workloads.

Some more context: https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/12602

title: Add support for pods to differentiate between a scale down and a shutdown events
body:
### Enhancement Description

- Support an optional lifecycle hook for signaling scale down
or
- Support a flag or argument to existing PreStop lifecycle hook to indicate scale down

#### Background

Currently, there is not a way for a workload running in pod to differentiate between a scale down and a shutdown. Pod shutdown down scenarios are common for upgrades, Kuberentes patching, or moving the pod to a different node for Node patching.

Maintenance windows would be lower for stateful workloads if they were able to  differentiate between scale down and shutdown in order to only handle draining or transferring of data during scale down, instead of having to drain for every shutdown scenario.

title: [NodeDeclaredFeatures] GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize version skew problem
body:
The `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` node declared feature isn't just tied to the `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate: it declares the feature if the feature gate is enabled OR the node doesn't use static CPU policy, and then requires the feature gate for all CPU resizes of guaranteed pods.

Here is the problem:
- v1.34 node: in-place pod resize is enabled, static policy disabled
	- 1.34 is pre-NDF, so it doesn't declare any features
- v1.35 control plane: NDF disabled (still alpha)
	- resizing guaranteed pod CPU is allowed (no NDF admission check), node doesn't mark resize as infeasible since it doesn't have static CPU policy.
- Upgrade cluster to v1.36: NDF goes beta & default enabled
	- Now resizing a guaranteed pod's CPU requires the `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, but the v1.34 node still doesn't set it, causing a regression.

I don't think we need to fix this in v1.35 since NDF is still alpha, but this is a beta-blocker.

/cc @natasha41575 
/milestone v1.36

title: Introduce Resource Size as a new Scalability Dimension
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I propose for the introduction of Resource Size as a formal scalability dimension in Kubernetes. The scalability testing is still based on an 8 year old assumption that pods are simple, single-container applications with a minimal resource footprint (tested pods are ~4 KB). However, the evolution of Kubernetes, the rise of machine learning workloads, and the adoption of patterns like init containers and sidecars have led to significantly larger pod objects in real-world scenarios.

This discrepancy creates a significant friction point for users who unexpectedly encounter a hard scalability wall, where a cluster with as few as 50 nodes can become unstable with large pods, despite our official support for 5,000-node clusters.

Recent advancements in the API server ([blogpost](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/09/kubernetes-v1-34-snapshottable-api-server-cache/)), particularly in caching, response streaming, and API Priority and Fairness ([#132233](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132233)), have substantially improved the control plane's ability to handle large resources . We are now in a strong position to formally address this gap, set an official goal for resource size scalability, and provide a more predictable experience for users running complex applications.

### Why is this needed?

When Kubernetes scalability goals were developed 7 years ago for the 1.6 release, the assumption was that most workloads would consist of simple, single-container applications. As a result, the size of the pod object itself was not considered a critical factor in scalability testing. Our official scalability tests for 5,000-node clusters still use pod objects of only 4 KB.

However, the Kubernetes ecosystem has evolved dramatically:
* Complex Application Architectures: Features like init containers, sidecars, and a growing number of environment variables have "supercharged" pod objects, making them much larger and more complex.
* Real-World Usage: We have observed that real-world pod sizes are often significantly larger than our tested scenarios, with pods averaging 10-20KB, and in some cases reaching even 100KB.
* A Surprising Scalability Cliff: While Kubernetes supports objects up to 1.5 MB, and our documentation states a 5,000-node scalability target, there is a practical, undocumented limit on pod size that users frequently and unexpectedly encounter. This leads to a poor user experience where they hit a hard scalability wall long before reaching documented limits for other dimensions like node or pod count.

The improvements in K8s 1.34 has shown that the API server can handle much larger resources efficiently. It's time to leverage these improvements to make resource size a first-class citizen in our scalability testing and guarantees.

## Proposed Plan

1. Enable Customization and Baseline Testing:
    * Add an option to customize resource size in our existing scalability tests.
    * Introduce a new, non-blocking scalability test with an increased resource size to establish a baseline and understand the current state of performance.
2. Document and Enforce:
    * Based on the initial findings, document the current realistic scalability threshold for resource size.
    * Promote the baseline test to be release-blocking to prevent regressions.
3. Iterate, Improve, and Decompose:
    * Begin a cycle of incrementally increasing the resource size in the non-blocking test.
    * With each increase, identify performance bottlenecks and address them.
    * As part of this process, develop component-specific benchmarks to isolate and analyze performance, similar to the ongoing work for LIST benchmarks ([#130169](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/130169)).
4. Define a Target:
    * Our proposed initial target is to **target support an average pod size of 100 KB** across our existing 150,000 pod scalability envelope. This goal represents only ~1/15th of the maximum object size supported,  making it resilient for large user application. At that level we expect the resource size will stop being concern for our users at all.
    * The initial target is soft goal that might be relaxed. The iterative nature of improvements should allow us to stop at any point, whether we encounter a hard blocker or reduction of active contributors.

By making resource size a formal dimension of our scalability envelope, we can provide a much more realistic and reliable experience for the Kubernetes community, ensuring that Kubernetes continues to be the best platform for running all types of workloads, from simple applications to complex, large-scale systems.

/sig scalability
/sig api-machinery 
/cc @wojtek-t @siyuanfoundation @liggitt @shyamjvs @marseel

title: kubelet: static pod manifest directory reads ALL non-hidden files — no extension filter in extractFromDir()
body:
### What happened

The kubelet's static pod file provider reads **all non-hidden files** from the manifest directory without any file extension filter. Common operations like backing up a manifest file before modifying it can silently cause incorrect static pod behavior.

**Example scenario:**

```bash
# Before modifying kube-apiserver, operator creates a backup:
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# Modify the manifest
sudo sed -i '...' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Result: backup file OVERRIDES the modified manifest
# The kubelet silently uses the old spec from the backup file
```

### Root Cause

In `pkg/kubelet/config/file.go`, the `extractFromDir()` function uses:

```go
dirents, err := filepath.Glob(filepath.Join(name, "[^.]*"))
```

The glob pattern `[^.]*` matches **any filename that doesn't start with a dot**. There is no extension filtering — files like `.backup`, `.bak`, `.orig`, `.tmp`, `.swp`, `notes.txt` are all read and parsed as Pod manifests.

When two files produce a Pod with the same name (e.g., `kube-apiserver.yaml` and `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup`):
1. `sort.Strings(dirents)` processes files alphabetically
2. The store uses `MetaNamespaceKeyFunc` (namespace/name) as the key
3. **Last file wins** — `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup` sorts after `kube-apiserver.yaml`
4. The backup's old spec silently overrides the modified manifest

### What you expected to happen

The kubelet should either:

**Option A:** Filter files by recognized extensions (`.yaml`, `.yml`, `.json`, `.manifest`) — consistent with how most tools handle config directories.

**Option B:** Warn in kubelet logs when non-standard files are found in the manifests directory.

**Option C:** At minimum, document this behavior prominently in the [static pod documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/) with a warning about backup files.

### How to reproduce

```bash
# 1. On a working kubeadm control plane node, list current manifests
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Output: etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

# 2. Record current kube-apiserver args
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: (default or current value)

# 3. Create a backup file INSIDE the manifests directory
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# 4. Modify the real manifest (add a visible flag)
sudo sed -i '/--tls-private-key-file/a\    - --request-timeout=300s' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 5. Wait for kubelet to process
sleep 30

# 6. Check running process — the change is NOT applied
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: (nothing — flag is missing because backup overrides the manifest)

# 7. Verify the manifest file DOES contain the change
sudo grep 'request-timeout' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Output: - --request-timeout=300s  (present in file, but not in running container)

# 8. Remove the backup file
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup
sleep 30

# 9. Now the change takes effect
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: --request-timeout=300s  (now applied)
```

### Real-world impact

We discovered this while deploying encryption at rest to 6 control plane nodes across 2 kubeadm clusters (Kubernetes v1.33.3). A backup file from a previous attempt (`kube-apiserver.yaml.backup-20260210`) was left in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on one node and silently prevented the encryption configuration from taking effect.

This is a particularly dangerous foot-gun because:
1. **Backing up before modifying is a best practice** — operators naturally create backups in the same directory
2. **The failure is completely silent** — no error, no warning, no log entry indicating the backup file was read
3. **The behavior is counterintuitive** — operators expect only `.yaml` files to be parsed as manifests
4. **Debugging is extremely difficult** — the manifest file shows the correct spec, but the running container uses the old spec from the backup

### Environment

```
Kubernetes:        v1.33.3
Container runtime: containerd 1.7.27
OS:                Rocky Linux 9 / Debian 12
Kubelet:           v1.33.3, installed via kubeadm
```

### Affected versions

This behavior has existed since the static pod file provider was introduced. The glob pattern `[^.]*` has been stable for many releases.

### Suggested fix

**Option A (recommended): Extension filtering**

```go
// In extractFromDir(), after the glob:
var manifests []string
for _, f := range dirents {
    ext := filepath.Ext(f)
    if ext == ".yaml" || ext == ".yml" || ext == ".json" || ext == ".manifest" {
        manifests = append(manifests, f)
    } else {
        klog.Warningf("Ignoring non-manifest file in static pod directory: %s", f)
    }
}
dirents = manifests
```

**Option B (minimum): Warning log**

```go
for _, f := range dirents {
    ext := filepath.Ext(f)
    if ext != ".yaml" && ext != ".yml" && ext != ".json" && ext != ".manifest" {
        klog.Warningf("Non-manifest file found in static pod directory: %s — "+
            "all non-hidden files are parsed as Pod manifests", f)
    }
}
```

### Related

- #136931 — kubelet: static pod manifest changes silently ignored (discovered this issue during investigation)
- #81122 — TOB-K8S-019: kubelet can cause OOM with malicious manifest (same code path)

title: kubelet: static pod manifest changes to command/args/volumes silently ignored — containerChanged() hash limited to name+image since PR #124220
body:
### What happened

When modifying static pod manifests on disk (e.g., adding `--encryption-provider-config` to kube-apiserver), the kubelet:
1. Detects the file change via inotify ✅
2. Reads the new spec from disk ✅
3. `podsDifferSemantically()` detects the spec changed ✅
4. Pod workers receive the update and call `SyncPod()` ✅
5. `computePodActions()` calls `containerChanged()` → returns **false** ❌
6. **No container restart occurs — old configuration persists** ❌

**Impact:** This prevents any post-deployment static pod configuration changes that don't involve an image change. Specifically tested and confirmed broken:
- Adding `--encryption-provider-config` flag (encryption at rest)
- Adding `volumeMounts` and `volumes`
- Any command-line flag additions/changes

Tested on **6 control plane nodes** across **2 independent clusters** (SIT and UAT), all running Kubernetes v1.33.3 with kubeadm.

### What you expected to happen

When a static pod manifest file is modified, the kubelet should detect spec changes and restart the affected container with the new configuration, as documented in the [Kubernetes static pod documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/).

### Root Cause Analysis

The bug involves two code-level issues that compound for static pods:

#### Primary: `pickFieldsToHash()` only hashes `name` and `image`

**File:** `pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go`

```go
// pickFieldsToHash pick fields that will affect the running status of the
// container for hash, currently this field range only contains `image` and `name`.
// Note: this list must be updated if ever kubelet wants to allow mutations to other fields.
func pickFieldsToHash(container *v1.Container) map[string]string {
    retval := map[string]string{
        "name":  container.Name,
        "image": container.Image,
    }
    return retval
}
```

This function was intentionally limited by **PR #124220** (merged May 2024) to prevent cluster-wide container restarts during API server upgrades that add new field defaults (fixes #122028, #63814). For regular pods with immutable specs, this is correct.

**For static pods, this is a breaking change:** Static pod manifests are mutable (edited on disk), and `containerChanged()` is the mechanism in `computePodActions()` that detects whether a running container's spec differs from the desired spec:

```go
// In computePodActions() — kuberuntime_manager.go:
if _, _, changed := containerChanged(&container, containerStatus); changed {
    message = fmt.Sprintf("Container %s definition changed", container.Name)
    restart = true
}
```

Since `containerChanged()` calls `HashContainer()` → `pickFieldsToHash()`, it only compares `name` and `image`. Adding `--encryption-provider-config` to the kube-apiserver command doesn't change name or image, so the hash is identical and `changed = false`.

#### Secondary: Static pod UID-based recreation doesn't compensate

`applyDefaults()` in `pkg/kubelet/config/common.go` computes the static pod UID from the full pod content via `hash.DeepHashObject(hasher, pod)`. When the manifest changes, a **new UID is generated**, which should trigger a full pod deletion and recreation. However, this mechanism is defeated by:
- Pod state reconstruction from `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<old-UID>/` on kubelet restart
- Mirror pod conflicts when the API server (served by other control plane nodes with old manifests) returns the old mirror pod spec

We observed in kubelet logs two different UIDs being processed simultaneously — the new UID from the file (with the encryption volume) and the old UID from the API server mirror pod (without it). The old UID's pod consistently wins.

### How to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Start with working Kubernetes v1.33.3 cluster (kubeadm)
kubectl version --short
# Server Version: v1.33.3

# 2. On a control plane node, create encryption config
sudo mkdir -p /etc/kubernetes/enc
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml > /dev/null <<EOF
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - secretbox:
          keys:
            - name: key-test
              secret: $(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
      - identity: {}
EOF

# 3. Backup and modify kube-apiserver manifest
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# Add encryption flag after --tls-private-key-file line
sudo sed -i '/--tls-private-key-file/a\    - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Add volumeMount (after the k8s-certs volumeMount block)
sudo sed -i '/name: k8s-certs$/a\    - mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/enc\n      name: enc\n      readOnly: true' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Add volume (after the k8s-certs volume block)
sudo sed -i '/^    name: k8s-certs$/a\  - hostPath:\n      path: /etc/kubernetes/enc\n      type: DirectoryOrCreate\n    name: enc' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 4. Wait for kubelet to process the change (~30 seconds)
sleep 30

# 5. VERIFY BUG: Manifest has config, container doesn't
echo "=== Manifest File (should contain flag) ==="
sudo grep 'encryption-provider-config' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Output: - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml ✓

echo "=== Running Container (flag is MISSING) ==="
sudo crictl inspect $(sudo crictl ps --name=kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -c encryption-provider-config
# Output: 0  ← BUG CONFIRMED

echo "=== Volume Mount (mount is MISSING) ==="
sudo crictl inspect $(sudo crictl ps --name=kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -c '/etc/kubernetes/enc'
# Output: 0  ← BUG CONFIRMED
```

**Additional verification — kubelet restart does NOT fix the issue:**
```bash
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sleep 30
sudo crictl inspect $(sudo crictl ps --name=kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -c encryption-provider-config
# Output: 0  ← Still missing after restart
```

### Environment

```
Kubernetes:       v1.33.3
Container runtime: containerd 1.7.27
OS:               Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm) / Rocky Linux 9
Kubelet:          v1.33.3, installed via kubeadm
Nodes tested:     6 control plane nodes across 2 clusters
```

### Affected versions

Verified via `git tag --contains f6b650430a75` against the kubernetes/kubernetes repository:
- **First affected:** v1.31.0-alpha.1 (commit `f6b650430a75`, PR #124220)
- **Confirmed affected:** v1.31.x, v1.32.x, v1.33.x (all releases)
- **NOT affected:** v1.30.x and earlier

### Affected Operations

This bug affects **any** static pod spec change that doesn't involve an image change:

| Change Type | Detected by `containerChanged()`? | Impact |
|-------------|-----------------------------------|--------|
| Image change | ✅ YES (hashed) | Works correctly |
| Container name change | ✅ YES (hashed) | Works correctly |
| **Command-line flags** | ❌ NO (not hashed) | **Flags silently ignored** |
| **Args** | ❌ NO (not hashed) | **Args silently ignored** |
| **Volumes** | ❌ NO (not hashed) | **Volumes silently ignored** |
| **VolumeMounts** | ❌ NO (not hashed) | **Mounts silently ignored** |
| **Environment variables** | ❌ NO (not hashed) | **Env vars silently ignored** |
| Network namespace | ✅ YES (checked by PodSandboxChanged) | Works correctly |

### Suggested Fix

The fix should preserve PR #124220's protection against upgrade-related restarts while properly handling static pod spec changes. Options:

**Option A: Expand `pickFieldsToHash()` for static pods** (targeted fix)

Add a static-pod-aware code path in `computePodActions()` that performs a full spec comparison when the pod source is a file:

```go
// In computePodActions():
if kubetypes.IsStaticPod(pod) {
    if _, _, changed := containerChanged(&container, containerStatus); !changed {
        // For static pods, also compare the full spec hash since
        // pickFieldsToHash only checks name+image (PR #124220)
        if expectedFullHash := hashFullContainerSpec(&container); expectedFullHash != containerStatus.FullSpecHash {
            message = fmt.Sprintf("Static pod container %s spec changed", container.Name)
            restart = true
        }
    }
}
```

**Option B: Ensure UID-based recreation works for static pods**

When a static pod manifest changes, the UID changes (computed by `DeepHashObject` in `applyDefaults()`). Ensure the kubelet properly handles this as a pod deletion + recreation, even when old pod state exists in `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/` or the mirror pod still exists in the API server.

**Option C: Store and compare container spec hash in sandbox annotations**

Store a hash of the full container spec when creating the sandbox, and compare on subsequent syncs:

```go
// When creating sandbox:
annotations["kubelet.kubernetes.io/container-spec-hash"] = computeFullSpecHash(container)

// In containerChanged():
if storedHash != computeFullSpecHash(container) {
    return true  // spec changed
}
```

### Related Issues and PRs

- **PR #124220** — `[kubelet]: fixed container restart due to pod spec field changes` (merged May 2024) — **introduced** the `pickFieldsToHash()` limitation that causes this bug for static pods
- **#122028** — Enabling InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate causes restart of containers
- **#63814** — kubelet's calculation of whether a container has changed can cause cluster-wide outages
- **#41476** — Kubelet does not react to changes in manifest files (2017)
- **#116597** — Kubelet does not sync pod updates for static pods (2023)
- **#118069** — kubeadm: static pod changes detection logic inconsistent (2023, v1.28.x)
- **#134908** — Static pod was not restarted after update (2025, v1.31, different symptom: volume unmount race)

/kind bug
/sig node
/area kubelet

### Workaround

Until this is fixed, the only reliable way to apply static pod manifest changes is to **change the container image tag** simultaneously (e.g., pin to the same image with a digest), which changes the hash and triggers a container restart. Alternatively, use `kubeadm upgrade` which handles manifest regeneration through a different code path.

body:

[Triage](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?date=2026-02-11&pr=1&text=TestUpdateNewNodeStatus&test=k8s.io%2Fkubernetes%2Fpkg%2Fkubelet&xjob=s3)

### Steps to Reproduce:

```
[root@kubetest2-tf1 kubernetes]# uname -a
Linux kubetest2-tf1.fyre.ibm.com 5.14.0-669.el9.x86_64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Jan 28 11:11:41 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

[root@kubetest2-tf1 kubernetes]# stress  ./kubelet.test -test.run '^TestUpdateNewNodeStatus$'
....
/tmp/go-stress-20260211T225317-658910838

I0211 22:53:18.020763   14915 state_mem.go:41] "Initialized" logger="cpu.fake.CPUManager state memory"
I0211 22:53:18.020779   14915 state_mem.go:36] "Initializing new in-memory state store" logger="memory-mgr.fake"
I0211 22:53:18.021848   14915 state_mem.go:36] "Initializing new in-memory state store" logger="memory-mgr.fake"
```
